intuition: Two lines form the sides of a container. Its area is their distance multiplied by the shorter height. Start with the widest pair. After measuring it, move the shorter side inward: keeping that short side and reducing the width cannot give a larger area.

Start with the widest possible pair. Suppose its left wall is shorter. Every narrower pair that keeps this wall has width no larger and water level no higher than this wall. None can beat the pair just measured. That entire family of candidates can therefore be discarded by advancing the left pointer.

The taller wall remains because a new, taller opposite wall might raise the limiting level enough to offset the reduced width. Apply the same argument symmetrically when the right wall is shorter. Measure before moving, keep a running maximum, and stop when no pair remains. Equal heights permit either pointer to move.

steps: For [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7], left=0 and right=8 give width 8, level 1, and area 8.
The left wall is shorter, so discard index 0. Indices 1 and 8 give width 7, level 7, and area 49.
Now the right wall is shorter. Move right to 7; the area falls to 6×3=18, so best stays 49.
Moving the shorter right wall again reaches index 6: width 5 and level 8 give area 40.
Equal heights at indices 1 and 6 let left advance. The remaining measured areas are 24, 6, 10, and 4: narrowing can raise or lower the area, but none beats 49. When pointers meet, return 49.

concept.question: Which wall can we safely discard after measuring a container?
intuition: Every pair of walls gives a possible container, so checking all pairs takes quadratic work. The widest pair is a useful starting point, but width alone is not enough: the shorter wall sets the water level.

Imagine a horizontal waterline between two walls. Its height is limited by the shorter wall. Moving the taller wall inward would reduce width without raising that limit. Instead, discard the shorter wall and look for a taller replacement.
concept.observation: Measure the area, then move a shorter wall inward. On equal heights, either wall can move.
approach: Begin at the two outermost walls.
Multiply their distance by the shorter height and remember the largest area.
Move the shorter side inward and repeat until the walls meet.
concept.correctness: When a wall is shorter, every container using that wall and an interior opposite wall has less width and a water level no greater than its height. None can improve its measured area. Discarding that wall therefore loses no better answer. Repeating this safe elimination leaves the maximum among the measured pairs.

complexity.explanation: Each move discards one wall, so there are fewer moves than walls. Only two positions and the largest area are remembered, giving linear work and constant extra memory.

pitfalls: Width is the difference of wall positions.
Move a shorter wall only after recording its area.
